summary_html: A **judge orders** CPS to investigate or assess during civil/criminal proceedings. Federal funding statutes (ASFA/IV-E) tether court findings to child-welfare actions, embedding judicial oversight into intake-to-case flow.
authority_html:
- **ASFA (42 U.S.C. §§ 671–675)** — court ‘reasonable efforts’ findings; permanency timelines  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funding structure linking court oversight to agency actions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case arising from a New Hampshire DCYS investigation and ex parte removal, the court affirmed dismissal of the 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against a court-appointed psychologist and her supervisor because the complaint stated no violation of any federal constitutional right, and affirmed dismissal of the state law claims as barred by the reporter immunity of RSA 169-C:31.
key_cases.relevance: The psychologist was acting under a district court order for counseling and reporting, which the court treated as sufficient to make her a state actor.
key_cases.quote: the relationship between parent and child may be investigated and terminated by the state provided constitutionally adequate procedures are followed

key_cases.case_name: In re J.H.; In re A.H.
key_cases.holding: The court held that after the neglect petitions against the father were dismissed the circuit court could maintain the children's out-of-home placement pending a parental fitness hearing at which the State bore the burden of rebutting his presumed fitness by a preponderance of the evidence, and that this process did not impermissibly burden his constitutional right to parent.
key_cases.relevance: The circuit court's own order directing a fitness inquiry, rather than a new agency petition, is the mechanism by which a judge reopens the child protection question.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that this process struck the proper balance between Father’s fundamental right to raise and care for his children and the State’s interest in protecting the children’s welfare

key_cases.holding: The court held that a natural or adoptive parent who has not been found to have abused or neglected his child may not be deprived of custody unless, after a full hearing, the State proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the parent abused or neglected the child or is otherwise unfit, and it reversed and remanded for that hearing.
key_cases.relevance: The district court itself directed DCYF to perform a home study and investigate the unnamed father, and the opinion fixes the process owed once a judge reopens the custody question that way.
key_cases.quote: we hold that parents who have not been charged with abuse or neglect be afforded, upon request, a full hearing in the district court regarding their ability to obtain custody

state_agency.name: Division for Children, Youth and Families
state_agency.hotline: 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only) or 603-271-6562; DCYF Central Intake is staffed 24 hours a day, including weekends and holidays

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 169-C:29
Physicians, surgeons, county medical examiners, psychiatrists, residents, interns
Registered nurses and hospital personnel (admission, examination, care and treatment)
Teachers, school officials, school nurses, school counselors
Social workers, day care workers, and any other child or foster care workers
reporting_details: New Hampshire is a universal-reporter state: RSA 169-C:29 lists physicians, dentists, psychologists, registered nurses and hospital personnel, teachers, school officials and school nurses, social workers, day care and other child or foster care workers, law enforcement officials and clergy, and closes with “any other person having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected,” all of whom “shall report the same in accordance with this chapter.” RSA 169-C:30 sets the route and the form: an oral report “shall be made immediately by telephone or otherwise, and followed within 48 hours by a report in writing, if so requested, to the department” — the Department of Health and Human Services, which takes reports through the DCYF Central Intake Unit at 603-271-6562 or 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only), staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays.

other: Parental incarceration; Caregiver self-harm; Parental mental health problems that prevent proper care; Hospitalization for physical illness

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately if the child’s immediate safety or well-being is endangered, the family may flee, or the child may disappear; otherwise within 72 hours
